title: Two separate things
sub: The Job System is threads, Burst is a compiler. People mix them up, and interviewers know it
cards/0/title: The Job System and Burst are not the same thing
cards/0/body:
A performance interview often opens with an easy one: “How is the Job System different from Burst?” The right answer: they are two independent things that work well together.

The Job System is about threads. You describe work as a job struct, and the engine spreads it over worker threads, respects the dependencies between jobs and, in the Editor, catches data races through the safety system.

Burst is about compilation. It is a compiler: it takes the IL of your C# and, through LLVM, turns it into native machine code for a specific CPU — with SIMD vector instructions that process 4–8 numbers in one operation. It does not compile all of C#, only a subset called HPC# (High-Performance C#): structs, primitives, native containers, no managed objects.

In short: the Job System answers “on which threads”, Burst answers “with what machine code”.
cards/1/body:
A job is a struct that implements a job interface; the simplest is IJob with a single Execute() method. The struct’s fields are its input and output.

The job gets a copy of the struct, so results come back only through a native container such as NativeArray<T>: its copy points at the same unmanaged memory. Fields cannot hold references to managed objects, and main-thread APIs (Time, transform, Physics) are not available inside a job — you pass what you need in fields, for example dt = Time.deltaTime. The [ReadOnly] attribute says the job only reads a field.

Schedule() queues the job and returns a JobHandle; Complete() waits for it to finish — only then may the main thread read the result.

A native container is allocated with an allocator and freed by hand with Dispose(): Allocator.TempJob lives a few frames, for a job; Allocator.Persistent lives long, for example for the lifetime of a component. Data and allocators are covered in unit 2, Schedule and Complete in lesson 4.
cards/2/options/0: Compiles a subset of C# (HPC#) through LLVM into native code with SIMD instructions
cards/2/options/1: Spreads jobs over the worker threads
cards/2/options/2: Looks for data races between jobs
cards/2/options/3: Speeds up any C# code, classes and LINQ included
cards/2/explain: Burst is a compiler, not a scheduler. It takes IL, hands it to LLVM and gets machine code for the target CPU. Threads, the queue and race checks come from the Job System.
cards/2/wrong/1: That is the Job System’s job: threads, the queue, dependencies. Burst knows nothing about threads.
cards/2/wrong/2: Races are caught by the Job System’s safety system — and only in the Editor.
cards/2/wrong/3: Burst compiles only HPC#: structs, primitives, native containers. Classes and LINQ are managed objects; it will not take them.
cards/3/body:
Since they are independent, there are four ways to combine them:

1. Plain C# on the main thread. The starting point: Mono or IL2CPP, one thread.

2. A job without Burst. The work moves to worker threads, but inside it is the same managed code. You gain parallelism, not better code.

3. Burst without worker threads. [BurstCompile] on a static method called from the main thread, or job.Run() — a Burst job executed right away on the current thread, with no queue. No extra threads, but the hot code is now native.

4. Job + Burst. Parallel and native — the usual choice for heavy loops.

Interviewers like it when you know about the third option: not every task is worth splitting across threads, but almost every hot numeric loop gains from Burst.
cards/4/body:
Burst compiles not only jobs but also static methods that you call directly from ordinary code. The rules are stricter than people expect:

— [BurstCompile] goes on the method and on the type that declares it;
— the method is static and not generic, and its declaring type is not generic either;
— parameters are primitives, pointers and structs only by ref, in or pointer: you cannot pass a struct by value, and results come back through out;
— most native containers, NativeArray included, cannot cross this boundary: they carry managed safety-system fields. You pass an array as a pointer and a length.

Under the hood a direct call becomes a call through a function pointer, and the transition has a cost: for a tiny method it can eat the gain. It pays to hand such a method a whole batch of work at once.
cards/5/q: You want to call a Burst method directly from the main thread. What does that require? Pick all that apply.
cards/5/options/0: [BurstCompile] on both the method and the class that declares it
cards/5/options/1: The method is static and not generic
cards/5/options/2: Structs are passed by ref, in or pointer
cards/5/options/3: The method is started with Schedule()
cards/5/options/4: A NativeArray is passed as a by-value parameter
cards/5/explain: A direct Burst call has nothing to do with jobs: no Schedule(), same thread. The attribute goes on the method and on the type, generics are not supported, structs go only by reference or pointer, and a NativeArray cannot cross the boundary because of its safety-system fields — you pass a pointer and a length.
cards/6/body:
Burst beats ordinary C# for several reasons at once:

— SIMD: a loop over a float array compiles to instructions that handle 4 (SSE, NEON) or 8 (AVX) numbers at a time;
— LLVM: aggressive optimizations — inlining, loop unrolling, hoisting invariants;
— code for the specific CPU and with no managed plumbing: no GC and no objects in the hot loop;
— data sits densely in native containers, so there are fewer cache misses.

You can see the result in the Burst Inspector (Jobs > Burst > Open Inspector): it shows the assembly of every job.

On number crunching — loops over arrays of numbers and vectors — the gain is usually several times, and on well-vectorized code it can be an order of magnitude. But at the interview quote your own number, measured: “Profile first, then Burst the hot loop.” If the bottleneck is not computation but, say, GameObject work, Burst will not help.
cards/6/deep: In the Editor Burst compiles asynchronously: until compilation finishes, the job runs as ordinary managed code. For measurements in the Editor turn on Jobs > Burst > Synchronous Compilation or use [BurstCompile(CompileSynchronously = true)], and let the code warm up. In a player build the code is always compiled ahead of time (AOT), so the setting does not exist there.
cards/7/q: A job is scheduled with Schedule() but has no [BurstCompile]. What do you get?
cards/7/options/0: Parallelism on worker threads, but inside it is ordinary managed code without Burst optimizations
cards/7/options/1: A compile error: a job must use Burst
cards/7/options/2: The same native code: Burst turns itself on for every job
cards/7/options/3: The job runs on the main thread
cards/7/explain: The Job System works without Burst — that is combination 2. You get the speed-up from threads but not from the compiler. In production, jobs are usually marked [BurstCompile] whenever the code fits HPC#.
cards/7/wrong/1: The Job System does not need Burst: a job without the attribute is ordinary managed code on a worker thread.
cards/7/wrong/2: Burst is switched on only by the [BurstCompile] attribute.
cards/7/wrong/3: Schedule() hands the job to the scheduler, and it is normally the worker threads that run it. Run() is what executes a job right away on the current thread.
cards/8/task: Move the loop from Update into a job: struct MoveJob : IJob with [BurstCompile], fields positions, velocities (with [ReadOnly]) and float dt. In Update create the job, pass Time.deltaTime into dt, call Schedule() and then Complete() (right after each other for now — lesson 4 spreads them across the frame). No loop should remain in Update.
cards/8/checks/0/label: MoveJob is an IJob struct with the [BurstCompile] attribute
cards/8/checks/2/label: MoveJob has a public float dt field
cards/8/checks/4/label: Update calls Schedule() and then Complete()
cards/8/checks/5/label: There is no for loop in Update
cards/8/explain: The loop body moved into Execute(), the data into the job’s fields. Time.deltaTime is read on the main thread and passed by value, because Unity APIs are not available in a job. [ReadOnly] on velocities says the job never changes that array. At the interview you put it the same way: data into native containers, the loop into Execute, the job under Burst, and Complete() as late as possible.
cards/9/q: Interviewer: “Why Burst, if you can just spread the work over threads?” Which answer is stronger?
cards/9/options/0: Threads split the work across cores, while Burst speeds up the code itself on each core — SIMD and LLVM optimizations. The effects add up
cards/9/options/1: Burst is not needed once the jobs are parallel
cards/9/options/2: Burst only matters on mobile devices
cards/9/options/3: Jobs do not work in a player build without Burst
cards/9/explain: On 8 cores threads give at most ~8x, and only with a perfect split. Burst speeds up every iteration. That is why a heavy loop usually gets combination 4 — a job plus Burst — and the numbers come from the profiler.
cards/9/wrong/1: Parallelism and code quality are independent axes: parallel managed code is still scalar and still carries managed plumbing.
cards/9/wrong/2: Burst generates code for x86 and ARM; the gain on desktop is just as real.
cards/9/wrong/3: A job without Burst works everywhere — it is ordinary managed code on a worker thread.
cards/10/q: Put the steps in order: moving a hot loop to Jobs + Burst.
cards/10/items/0: Find the hot loop in the profiler
cards/10/items/1: Move the data into a NativeArray
cards/10/items/2: Move the loop body into Execute() of a job struct
cards/10/items/4: Measure again and compare with the original
cards/10/explain: Measure first, or you may speed up the wrong thing. Then data into native containers, the loop into a job, Burst — and measure again: “Profile first, then Burst the hot loop.”
